newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Top Russian art museum unable to pay bills.
newsitem.headline: Top Russian art museum unable to pay bills.

text.p: The Tretyakov Gallery, home of the world's greatest collection of Russian art, is unable to pay its bills and could find its electricity switched off for non-payment, its director said on Tuesday.
"There is that danger, yes, there is that danger," Valentin Rodionov told Reuters, referring to a possible shutdown by Moscow's electric company.
"For the first time in our history, we're in debt," Rodionov said after a news conference outlining the museum's financial woes. "But we are begging everybody not to take extreme measures."

Home to one of the world's great collections of medieval icons and the country's leading Russian masterpieces, the Tretyakov reopened in 1995 after a decade-long renovation gave it an impressive, modern makeover.

But a reduction of government subsidies has left the museum strapped financially, and as of the beginning of this year it was 15 billion roubles ($2.7 million) in debt, said Irina Merkulova, the museum's deputy director and chief economist.
It owes 10.7 billion roubles ($1.9 million) to Moscow utilities, she said, a debt which Rodionov said raised the spectre of an electricity blackout.
"We are using convincing words and perhaps some personal connections as we try to get rid of this problem," Rodionov said.
Merkulova added: "We are now faced with a dilemma -- either we pay off our debts or we pay our current operating expenses."

Although it is hard to believe utilities would pull the plug on the capital's leading museum, Russian electric companies have shut down supplies to the military and other institutions sacred during Soviet times who were unable to pay bills.
Many Russian museums try to avoid high electricity bills by keeping the lights off in each room until visitors arrive.
An official at Mosenergonadzor, which oversees overdue payments to Moscow's electric company, said they would never pull the plug on the exhibition rooms of the Tretyakov.
But the official, who asked not to be named, added that it could conceivably shut down administrative offices in an effort to prompt the government to help the museum with more subsidies.
Museum director Rodionov blamed many of his financial troubles on the government, which he said did not give the Tretyakov 35 billion roubles ($6.2 million) it had promised for 1996.

One bright area of the museum's finances has been growing contributions from corporate sponsors. Last year they received seven percent of their budget from private companies, and they are confident the number will grow.
"When we started the sponsorship programme attracted only foreign companies because they understood what sponsorship was," Merkulova said. "Then Russians started giving as well."
